pos: n. (Saxon city on the Elbe; the city that refused the Interim, and the city destroyed in 1631)
etymology: From Old High German Magadoburg, the maiden's fortress; Latin Magdeburgum.
biblical_def: Magdeburg was called our Lord God's chancery, and it earned the name twice. Luther went to school there as a boy, and the city reformed early and thoroughly; when the Emperor imposed the Augsburg Interim in 1548 and the other Saxon cities submitted, Magdeburg refused, was put under the ban, stood a siege, and became the press of the resistance — it was from Magdeburg that Matthias Flacius issued the Magdeburg Centuries, the first great Protestant church history. Eighty years later, in May 1631, Tilly's imperial army took the city by storm and burned it, and something like twenty thousand of its people died. The dictionary records Magdeburg because the two facts belong together: the city that would not bend is the city that was destroyed, and Scripture never promises otherwise. “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10) is addressed to a congregation told plainly that it will suffer first.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tribulation as severe affliction and distresses of life, a martyr as one who suffers death in defence of the truth, and a siege as the setting of an army before a fortified place to compel it to surrender.
webster_full: TRIBULA'TION, n. Severe affliction; distresses of life; vexations.
MARTYR, n. One who suffers death in defense of the truth, particularly of the Christian faith.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling it to surrender.
CROWN, n. An ornament worn on the head by kings and sovereign princes, as a badge of imperial or regal power.
scriptures: Rev 2:10

Fear none of those things which thou shalt suffer: behold, the devil shall cast some of you into prison, that ye may be tried; and ye shall have tribulation ten days: be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Rom 8:36
As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
Psa 79:1
A Psalm of Asaph. O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps.
Lam 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
corruption_summary: The city that refused the Augsburg Interim and printed the Magdeburg Centuries, and the city Tilly burned in 1631.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the half-conscious expectation that faithfulness will be rewarded in this life with safety, so that a church which suffers catastrophe is assumed to have deserved it or to have been mistaken. Magdeburg refused the Interim and was right to refuse it, and the refusal cost the city its existence.

The principle to recover is that the promised reward is a crown and not a reprieve. The letter to Smyrna sets the suffering and the reward side by side: “be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life” (Rev 2:10). Paul quotes the psalm as a settled description of the church's condition: “For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Rom 8:36). Scripture gives the lament its own words — “they have laid Jerusalem on heaps” (Psa 79:1) — and teaches the church to grieve a ruined city out loud: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1).

“How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1) — twenty thousand dead in our Lord God's chancery.

pos: n. (free Hanse city and archbishopric on the Weser; a Lutheran city that became Reformed over the Lord's Supper)
etymology: From Old Saxon Bremon, perhaps at the edge or brim; Latin Brema.
biblical_def: Bremen changed confession twice and both times over the Supper. It reformed as a Lutheran city in the 1520s, and then from 1547 its cathedral preacher Albert Hardenberg taught the Reformed doctrine of the sacrament; the quarrel ran for a decade, Hardenberg was expelled in 1561, and within a generation the city had followed him anyway, adopting a Reformed order and in 1595 the Bremen Consensus. The dictionary records Bremen because the city was willing to spend ten years on one question, having judged that how Christ is present to His people in the ordinance is not a detail. The Reformed answer is the one the dictionary holds: the bread and the cup are a true communion of the body and blood of Christ to the believer by faith, and not a sacrifice, and not a change of substance. “The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?” (1Co 10:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines communion as fellowship and intercourse, and the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper; a sacrament as, among the ancient Romans, an oath taken by soldiers to be true to their general.
webster_full: COMMU'NION, n. Fellowship; intercourse between two persons or more; the body of Christians who partake of the Lord's supper.
SACRAMENT, n. Among the ancient Romans, an oath taken by soldiers to be true to their general.
BREAD, n. A mass of dough, made by moistening and kneading the flour or meal of some species of grain, and baked in an oven.
SUPPER, n. The evening meal. People who dine at noon call their evening meal supper.
scriptures: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
corruption_summary: A Hanse city that spent a decade on the Lord's Supper, expelled Hardenberg, and then followed him into the Reformed confession.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruptions of the Supper are live on every side. Rome teaches a change of substance and a propitiatory sacrifice offered by a priest; the Lutheran formula locates the body in, with and under the elements; and a wide modern evangelicalism has emptied the ordinance in the other direction, treating it as a bare remembrance in which nothing is received and little is risked. All three are named here as departures.

The principle to recover is that the ordinance is a true communion in which Christ is received spiritually by faith. Paul calls it exactly that: “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ?” (1Co 10:16). It is also a proclamation bounded by time: “ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26). The institution is plain and was given with the Lord's own body still at the table: “Take, eat; this is my body” (Mat 26:26). And the manner of receiving is spiritual, on His own authority: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63).

“ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” (1Co 11:26) — expelled in 1561, and the city followed him.
“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — the Bremen Consensus of 1595.

pos: n. (free Hanse city on the Elbe; reformed 1529 under its first superintendent Johannes Aepinus)
etymology: From Old Saxon Hammaburg, the fortress on the bend or pasture; Latin Hamburgum.
biblical_def: Hamburg reformed in 1529 and then spent four centuries being rich. Johannes Aepinus, its first superintendent, had the church order drawn up and the schools founded; the city held to the Augsburg Confession, took in Dutch Reformed and English merchant congregations with their own worship, and became the greatest port of northern Germany. That combination — a confessional Lutheran city whose whole business was foreign trade — put the stewardship question to it continuously, and Hamburg answered it better than most: its poor relief, its orphanage and its endowments for the maintenance of preaching were among the best administered in Europe. The dictionary records Hamburg because wealth is a trust and not a verdict. “thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18) is the text for a trading city, and the warning beside it is the one Paul gave Timothy for the rich.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a merchant as a man who carries on trade with foreign countries, riches as possessions of land, goods or money in abundance, and a steward as a man employed to manage the concerns of a household.
webster_full: MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries.
RICHES, n. pl. 1. Wealth; opulence; affluence; possessions of land, goods, or money in abundance. 2. That which makes rich, as moral or spiritual qualities.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns of the household.
COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess.
scriptures: Deu 8:18
But thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth, that he may establish his covenant which he sware unto thy fathers, as it is this day.
The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it.
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
corruption_summary: Reformed in 1529 under Aepinus; the greatest northern port, and a trading city that administered its poor relief well.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse comes in two forms that Hamburg met daily. One treats prosperity as evidence of divine approval, so that the rich congregation assumes its own soundness; the other treats commerce itself as unclean, so that trade is left to men who have no doctrine at all. Neither is the biblical position.

The principle to recover is that the power to get wealth is itself a gift, held in trust, and that the giver is to be remembered in the getting. The command is express: “thou shalt remember the LORD thy God: for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth” (Deu 8:18). Where riches are His blessing they come without a sting: “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it” (Pro 10:22). The rich are charged to shift their confidence, not to abandon their calling: “that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God” (1Ti 6:17). And the Lord draws the boundary: “a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth” (Luk 12:15).

roots_lines: Hebrew chayil (H2428) — strength, substance, wealth; Deuteronomy 8:18.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember deliberately; Deuteronomy 8:18.

Greek hupselophroneo (G5309) — to be highminded, to think loftily; 1 Timothy 6:17.
Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the craving for more; Luke 12:15.

“that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches” (1Ti 6:17) — Dutch and English congregations in the port.
“beware of covetousness” (Luk 12:15) — poor relief, orphanage and endowed preaching.

pos: n. (free Hanse city on the Baltic, German Lubeck; reformed in 1531 by Bugenhagen's church order)
etymology: From a Slavic root Liubice, the lovely place; German Lubeck, Latin Lubeca.
biblical_def: Lubeck was the head of the Hanseatic League and the first of the great northern cities to reform, adopting in 1531 a church order drawn up by Johannes Bugenhagen, Luther's pastor at Wittenberg. The Reformation there arrived with a popular revolution: the burgomaster Jurgen Wullenwever, raised by the evangelical guilds, used the city's fleet to meddle in the Danish succession, overreached catastrophically, lost the war, was deposed in 1535 and executed in 1537, and Lubeck's commercial primacy never recovered. The church order outlived him by three centuries. The dictionary records Lubeck because the Reformation in that city was genuine and its political vehicle was ruinous, and because Scripture explains the ruin without ambiguity: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pride as inordinate self-esteem and an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority, haughty as proud and disdainful with contempt of others, and ambition as a desire of superiority or distinction.
webster_full: PRIDE, n. 1. Inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one’s own superiority in talents, beauty, wealth, accomplishments, rank or elevation in office.
HAUGHTY, a. Proud and disdainful; having a high opinion of one's self, with contempt of others.
AMBITION, n. A desire of preferment or honor; a desire of superiority or distinction.
HUMBLE, a. Low; opposed to high or lofty; not proud; submissive.
scriptures: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.
Jam 4:6
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.
Oba 1:3
The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee, thou that dwellest in the clefts of the rock, whose habitation is high; that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me down to the ground?
corruption_summary: Head of the Hanse, reformed by Bugenhagen's order in 1531; and Wullenwever's revolution, which cost the city its primacy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a right cause sanctifies the ambition of the man who carries it, so that boldness is read as faith and overreach as vision. Wullenwever was on the evangelical side and he wrecked his city.

The principle to recover is that pride is answered by God Himself and that the answer is a fall. The proverb states the sequence as a law: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18). The outcome reverses the man's own calculation: “A man's pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit” (Pro 29:23). God is named as the active opponent: “God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6). And the self-deception is the heart of it: “The pride of thine heart hath deceived thee” (Oba 1:3).
roots_summary: Hebrew gaon (H1347), pride and swelling; Hebrew shaphal (H8213), to bring low.
roots_lines: Hebrew gaon (H1347) — swelling, arrogance, pride; Proverbs 16:18.
Hebrew gobah (H1363) — height, haughtiness of spirit; Proverbs 16:18.
Hebrew shaphal (H8213) — to be low, to be brought low; Proverbs 29:23.
Greek antitassomai (G498) — to set oneself against, to resist; James 4:6.
Hebrew zadon (H2087) — presumption, insolent pride; Obadiah 3.
usage: “Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18) — Bugenhagen's church order of 1531.
“A man's pride shall bring him low” (Pro 29:23) — Wullenwever deposed 1535, executed 1537.
“God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble” (Jam 4:6) — a commercial primacy never recovered.

pos: n. (Hanse city and Mecklenburg university founded 1419; the chair of David Chytraeus)
etymology: From a Slavic root for the parting of a stream, rostok; German Rostock.
biblical_def: Rostock had the oldest university on the Baltic, and in the second half of the sixteenth century it had David Chytraeus, who taught there for forty-six years. Chytraeus was one of the six authors of the Formula of Concord, wrote the church orders of Austria and Styria, and was so widely consulted that he was called the reformer of the lands beyond the Elbe; he was also, in his own city, a reorganiser of schools, which he regarded as the same work by a quieter means. The dictionary records Rostock because a theologian of that rank spent his life catechising the young of a provincial port, and knew what he was doing. The deposit is handed on by instruction or it is not handed on. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6), and the generation that fails to teach has already decided what the next one will believe.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion, nurture as education and the discipline and admonition of the Lord, and admonition as counselling against a fault and instruction in duties.
webster_full: CAT'ECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
NURTURE, n. That which nourishes; education; instruction; the discipline and admonition of the Lord.
ADMONITION, n. Gentle reproof; counseling against a fault; instruction in duties; caution; direction.
CHILD, n. A son or a daughter; a male or female descendant, of any degree of distance from the parent.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: The oldest Baltic university, and David Chytraeus, Formula of Concord author, who spent forty-six years catechising a provincial port.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of serious theology from the teaching of children, so that the best minds write for one another and the catechising is left to whoever is available. Chytraeus wrote confessions for empires and school orders for Rostock, and treated them as one task.

The principle to recover is that the faith is transmitted by deliberate instruction of the young, and that the duty lies on fathers first. The proverb states the method and its durability: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). The psalmist makes it a refusal to be silent: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). The charge is domestic and specific — “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4) — and it begins very early: “that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15).
roots_summary: Hebrew chanak (H2596), to train or dedicate; Greek paideia (G3809), nurture and discipline.
roots_lines: Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to train, to dedicate, to initiate; Proverbs 22:6.
Hebrew naar (H5288) — a child, a youth under instruction; Proverbs 22:6.
Greek paideia (G3809) — nurture, training by discipline; Ephesians 6:4.
Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition, instruction by warning; Ephesians 6:4.
Greek brephos (G1025) — an infant, a babe; 2 Timothy 3:15.
usage: “Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — Chytraeus in the chair for forty-six years.
“We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4) — the church orders of Austria and Styria.
“that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15) — and the school orders of one Baltic port.

pos: n. (Hanse city on the Pomeranian coast; reformed in 1525, and besieged by Wallenstein in 1628)
etymology: From Low German Stralesund, the arrow sound, from the strait it guards.
biblical_def: Stralsund reformed in 1525 under Christian Ketelhot and Johannes Kureke, among the earliest of the Baltic towns, and a century later it did something no one expected. In 1628 Wallenstein brought the imperial army to its walls and swore he would take the place though it were chained to heaven; the city, reinforced by Danish and Swedish troops from the sea, held out through the summer and he withdrew. It was the first serious check the imperial advance had received, and it opened the way for Gustavus Adolphus to land in Germany two years later. The dictionary records Stralsund as the companion entry to Magdeburg, and the pairing is the point: one faithful city was burned and one was delivered, and neither outcome was the measure of its faith. The refuge is not the wall. “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fortress as any fortified place, a stronghold, refuge as shelter or protection from danger or distress, and a tower as a building raised to a considerable elevation for defence.
webster_full: FOR'TRESS, n. Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a stronghold.
REFUGE, n. Shelter or protection from danger or distress; that which shelters or protects.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation, for defence or ornament.
SIEGE, n. The setting of an army around or before a fortified place for the purpose of compelling it to surrender.
scriptures: Psa 46:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, A Song upon Alamoth. God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Psa 18:2
The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer; my God, my strength, in whom I will trust; my buckler, and the horn of my salvation, and my high tower.
The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe.
Nah 1:7
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
corruption_summary: Reformed in 1525, and the city that broke Wallenstein's siege in 1628, opening the way for the Swedish landing.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reading of deliverance as a verdict — the city that held believed rightly, the city that fell did not. Stralsund held and Magdeburg burned, and the two cities confessed the same faith. The outcome of a siege is providence, not a scorecard.

The principle to recover is that the refuge is God Himself and not the defence He may or may not grant. The psalm names Him directly: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1). The imagery of walls and towers is taken up and applied to Him: “The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2). The strong tower is a name, not a structure: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). And the promise is that He knows His own in the day itself: “he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nah 1:7).

roots_lines: Hebrew machaseh (H4268) — a shelter, a place of refuge; Psalm 46:1.
Hebrew oz (H5797) — strength, might, a stronghold; Psalm 46:1.
Hebrew metsudah (H4686) — a fastness, a fortress; Psalm 18:2.
Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower, a lofty defence; Proverbs 18:10.
Hebrew maoz (H4581) — a stronghold, a place of safety; Nahum 1:7.
usage: “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (Psa 46:1) — reformed 1525 under Ketelhot and Kureke.
“The LORD is my rock, and my fortress, and my deliverer” (Psa 18:2) — the siege of 1628 broken off.
“he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nah 1:7) — and Gustavus Adolphus landed two years later.

pos: n. (Hanse city of Mecklenburg; reformed from 1523, and later the seat of the Swedish high tribunal)
etymology: From a Slavic personal name with the suffix mir, peace; German Wismar.
biblical_def: Wismar heard evangelical preaching from Heinrich Never in 1523 and was formally reformed by 1526, one of the three Mecklenburg Hanse towns. Its second career was judicial: after the Peace of Westphalia the city passed to Sweden, and from 1653 it housed the Tribunal of Wismar, the supreme court for the Swedish possessions in Germany, which sat there for a century and a half and acquired a reputation for slow, careful and incorruptible judgment. The dictionary records Wismar because the pairing of a reformed church and a competent court in one small town illustrates what the Reformation expected of the civil order: not piety from the magistrate's bench, but justice. “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8) is addressed to a man, and a court is one of the places a man does it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justice as the virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due, judgment as the sentence pronounced on any person or thing, and mercy as the disposition that tempers justice.
webster_full: JUS'TICE, n. The virtue which consists in giving to every one what is his due; practical conformity to the laws and to principles of rectitude.
JUDGMENT, n. The sentence or doom pronounced on any person or thing.
MERCY, n. That benevolence, mildness or tenderness of heart which disposes a person to overlook injuries, or to treat an offender better than he deserves; the disposition that tempers justice.
OPPRESS, v.t. [L. oppressus.] To burden; to overburden; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Amo 5:24
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Isa 1:17
Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Pro 21:3
To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.
corruption_summary: A Mecklenburg Hanse town reformed from 1523, and the seat of the Swedish Tribunal of Wismar from 1653.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern transfer of the word justice from what a court does to what a movement demands, so that giving every man his due in a particular case — which is the whole of the magistrate's work — is treated as too small to be called by the name. A tribunal that decides slowly and cannot be bought is doing the thing Scripture names.

The principle to recover is that justice is a requirement laid on persons in office, with mercy and humility beside it. The summary is comprehensive and personal: “what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?” (Mic 6:8). The prophet asks for it in volume: “let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream” (Amo 5:24). Its objects are named and they are the ones least able to pay: “relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isa 1:17). And it is weighed above ceremony: “To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice” (Pro 21:3).

roots_lines: Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, a verdict, justice administered; Micah 6:8.
Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, covenant kindness; Micah 6:8.
Hebrew tsanea (H6800) — to be humble, to walk modestly; Micah 6:8.
Hebrew tsedaqah (H6666) — righteousness, right dealing; Amos 5:24.
Hebrew chamots (H2541) — the oppressor, or the oppressed one wronged; Isaiah 1:17.

“let judgment run down as waters” (Amo 5:24) — the Tribunal of Wismar from 1653.
“To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice” (Pro 21:3) — a court that could not be bought.

pos: n. (Saxon city, German Braunschweig; reformed in 1528 by Bugenhagen's order, and Chemnitz's superintendency)
biblical_def: Brunswick had two of the best church administrators of the century. Johannes Bugenhagen wrote its church order in 1528, the first of the series by which he organised the Reformation in Hamburg, Lubeck, Pomerania, Denmark and Norway; and from 1554 Martin Chemnitz served the city, as coadjutor and then as superintendent, for thirty-three years. Chemnitz was the greatest Lutheran theologian after Luther — the Examination of the Council of Trent is his — and he did that work while visiting parishes, examining candidates and settling parish quarrels in one middling Saxon city. The dictionary records Brunswick because the oversight of a flock is the office, and theological eminence is an addition to it rather than a substitute for it. “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the church as a congregation of Christians associated in one body in a particular place, an overseer as one who overlooks or superintends, and a flock as a collection of sheep.
webster_full: CHURCH, n. A congregation of Christians associated in one body, in a particular place, united under one form of ecclesiastical government.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a supervisor.
FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals.
PILLAR, n. A kind of irregular column, round and insulated; a monument raised to preserve memory.
scriptures: Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
But if I tarry long, that thou mayest know how thou oughtest to behave thyself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
Tit 2:1
But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine:
Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.
corruption_summary: Bugenhagen's church order of 1528, and Martin Chemnitz superintendent of the city for thirty-three years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern separation of the scholar from the pastor, in which the man who can write is excused from visiting and the man who visits is not expected to read. Chemnitz answered Trent and examined ordinands in the same working week.

The principle to recover is that the office is oversight of a particular flock, purchased at a price that fixes its value. Paul states both: “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28). The congregation has a public character to maintain: it is “the church of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15). The content of the ministry is prescribed — “speak thou the things which become sound doctrine” (Tit 2:1) — and the man and the doctrine are watched together: “Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them” (1Ti 4:16).
roots_summary: Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek poimaino (G4165), to shepherd.
roots_lines: Greek episkopos (G1985) — an overseer, a bishop, the elder's office; Acts 20:28.
Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend as a shepherd, to feed; Acts 20:28.
Greek peripoieomai (G4046) — to purchase, to acquire for oneself; Acts 20:28.
Greek stulos (G4769) — a pillar, a supporting column; 1 Timothy 3:15.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound, of doctrine in health; Titus 2:1.
usage: “to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers” (Act 20:28) — Bugenhagen's order of 1528.
“the pillar and ground of the truth” (1Ti 3:15) — Chemnitz superintendent from 1554.
“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine” (1Ti 4:16) — Trent answered between parish visitations.

pos: n. (free imperial city of the Harz; reformed in 1528, and ruined by its quarrel over the Rammelsberg mines)
etymology: From Old High German Goslar, from the Gose stream and a word for a dwelling.
biblical_def: Goslar reformed in 1528 and spent the next century losing its patrimony. The city's wealth was the Rammelsberg, a mountain of silver, lead and copper worked since the tenth century, and its Reformation coincided with a long struggle against Duke Henry of Brunswick, who wanted the mine. Goslar was placed under the imperial ban in 1540, defended itself through the Schmalkaldic War, and in the treaty of 1552 surrendered the Rammelsberg and its forests to the dukes; the imperial city survived in name and in poverty until 1802. The dictionary records Goslar because the plain shape of the story is Naboth's: a small holder, a powerful neighbour, and an inheritance the neighbour means to have. “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3) is the refusal; the loss that follows is the usual sequel in this world.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inheritance as an estate derived from an ancestor to an heir, and in Scripture the portion of a tribe in the land; a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land; and to covet as to desire that which it is unlawful to possess.
webster_full: INHERITANCE, n. An estate derived from an ancestor to an heir by succession; in Scripture, the portion of a tribe in the land.
LAND'MARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object.
COVET, v.t. To desire inordinately; to desire that which it is unlawful to obtain or possess.
OPPRESS, v.t. [L. oppressus.] To burden; to overburden; to treat with unjust severity, rigor or hardship.
scriptures: And Naboth said to Ahab, The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee.
Mic 2:2
And they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away: so they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
Isa 5:8
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
corruption_summary: Reformed in 1528, under imperial ban from 1540, and stripped of the Rammelsberg mines by treaty in 1552.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of inherited property as a mere asset, so that the taking of a family's or a community's patrimony is weighed only by efficiency. Scripture treats an inheritance as a trust across generations, and its seizure as a particular kind of sin with a particular name.

The principle to recover is that an inheritance is not simply saleable and that the powerful neighbour who means to have it is condemned. Naboth's answer is the model of a lawful refusal: “The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee” (1Ki 21:3). The prophet describes the method exactly: “they covet fields, and take them by violence; and houses, and take them away” (Mic 2:2). The accumulation itself is a woe: “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place” (Isa 5:8). And the boundary is not to be moved: “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28).
roots_summary: Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew gebul (H1366), a boundary.
roots_lines: Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a heritable portion; 1 Kings 21:3.
Hebrew chamad (H2530) — to desire, to covet; Micah 2:2.
Hebrew gazal (H1497) — to tear away, to take by violence; Micah 2:2.
Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, to defraud; Micah 2:2.
Hebrew gebul (H1366) — a border, a boundary, a landmark; Proverbs 22:28.
usage: “the inheritance of my fathers” (1Ki 21:3) — the Rammelsberg, worked since the tenth century.
“they covet fields, and take them by violence” (Mic 2:2) — the imperial ban of 1540.
“Remove not the ancient landmark” (Pro 22:28) — the mine and forests surrendered by treaty, 1552.

pos: n. (Hanse city of the salt trade; reformed from 1530 under Duke Ernest the Confessor and Urbanus Rhegius)
etymology: From Old Saxon Luniburg, from the Luhe stream and a word for a fortress; German Luneburg.
biblical_def: Luneburg was built on salt. Its brine springs supplied the whole Baltic herring trade through the Hanse, and the salt made the city rich enough to buy and keep its liberties. The Reformation came to it from above and below at once: the townsmen pressed for evangelical preaching through the 1520s, and Duke Ernest of Brunswick-Luneburg, called the Confessor because he signed the Augsburg Confession, brought in Urbanus Rhegius as his superintendent, who ordered the churches of the duchy from 1530 until his death in 1541. The dictionary records Luneburg for the plainest of reasons: a city whose entire fortune was a preservative is the natural place to set down what the Lord said about salt. “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted?” (Mat 5:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines salt as the muriate of soda used to season and preserve food, savour as taste or odour, something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste, and season as a fit or suitable time.
webster_full: SALT, n. Common salt is the muriate of soda, used to season and preserve food.
SAVOUR, n. 1. Taste or odour; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste or smell.
SEASON, n. One of the four divisions of the year, spring, summer, autumn, winter; a fit or suitable time.
MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries.
scriptures: Mat 5:13
Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing, but to be cast out, and to be trodden under foot of men.
Mar 9:50
Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his saltness, wherewith will ye season it? Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another.
Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be seasoned?
Col 4:6
Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.
corruption_summary: The salt city of the Hanse, reformed from 1530 under Duke Ernest the Confessor and Urbanus Rhegius.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the sentimental reading of the salt saying as a compliment to Christians rather than a warning to them. The Lord's point is the loss of savour and what becomes of the residue, and He says it to disciples, not about outsiders.

The principle to recover is that the church preserves the world around it by being distinctly what it is, and that a church indistinguishable from its surroundings has no further use. The warning is express: “Ye are the salt of the earth: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be salted? it is thenceforth good for nothing” (Mat 5:13). The remedy is internal before it is social: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another” (Mar 9:50). The question is asked again as if it could not be heard too often — “Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his savour, wherewith shall it be seasoned?” (Luk 14:34) — and it reaches as far as a man's ordinary conversation: “Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6).
roots_summary: Greek halas (G217), salt; Greek moraino (G3471), to make insipid or foolish.
roots_lines: Greek halas (G217) — salt, the seasoning and preservative; Matthew 5:13.
Greek moraino (G3471) — to make insipid, to lose savour; Matthew 5:13.
Greek katapateo (G2662) — to tread down under foot; Matthew 5:13.
Greek analos (G358) — saltless, without savour; Mark 9:50.
Greek artuo (G741) — to season, to make savoury; Colossians 4:6.
usage: “Ye are the salt of the earth” (Mat 5:13) — the brine springs that supplied the Hanse.
“Have salt in yourselves, and have peace one with another” (Mar 9:50) — Duke Ernest, who signed at Augsburg.
“Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt” (Col 4:6) — Rhegius superintendent, 1530 to 1541.
